title: My Father's Courage
translation_notes: The source JSON contains extraction units rather than reliable authorial paragraph boundaries. English literary units are reconstructed from syntax, narrative movement and verse form; the interventions are recorded in the source-note sidecar.
The repeated Tamil chapter heading at the beginning of the first extraction unit is represented by title metadata rather than repeated as body prose.
The source-unit joins 'கேட்க-' + 'லாம்' and 'விடு-' + 'மல்லவா?' are read continuously and disclosed in the source notes.

The extracted question 'அதன் வயிற்றுப் பசியை பார் போக்குவது?' is rendered contextually as asking who is to relieve the infant's hunger; the anomalous source form is explicitly documented rather than silently corrected.

Muthuvelar's satirical songs are retained as verse blocks inside the paragraph stream. Several lexical readings in the longer ஏலேலோ passage remain flagged for T2/source review; T1 therefore stays deliberately conservative there.
The final two source extraction units are Wikisource maintenance notices and are excluded from the literary translation as non-authorial material.
paragraphs: Ayyathurai and Periya Nayagathammal were living their married life together when, as a token of their love, she became pregnant. Filled with the joy that his wife was to become a mother and that he was to become a father, Ayyathurai had worship performed at every great temple and little village deity in the region. He conducted archanas. He made offerings and ritual spreads. The people of the village rejoiced when they heard the happy news.

As expected, the child was born—a very beautiful child. On the seventh day after the birth, nature claimed the child's mother, Periya Nayagathammal. Unable to bear the pain of losing his wife, the grief-stricken father too closed his eyes in the second month.

Having lost them both, that green little infant lay there without a care for anything. It cried only when hunger scorched its belly. Who was to relieve that hunger? How was it to be relieved? The story that Parvati came and gave milk to the weeping Thirugnana Sambandar on the bank of a tank and satisfied his hunger is a story—it is not everyday reality.

But in those days there was no shortage of affection in Thirukkuvalai. Two noble women, Thillaiyammal and Meenakshi, took upon themselves the responsibility of raising the child. People say a child grows in body by the day and in beauty by the hour; just so did that child grow upon their laps and shoulders.

Perhaps it was the joy of having found a pearl; or perhaps because the pearl comes into being at the cost of the shell—I do not know. They named the child Muthuvel. I tell you, with a deep sigh: “That child was my father.”

My father was a good farmer; a fine vidwan; a poet gifted with the power to write verse; and a man with particular learning in Sanskrit texts. He could tell the stories of the Bharata and the Ramayana more beautifully than many a pandit. He composed many true stories out of incidents in the village. Even today, one can hear people in Thirukkuvalai singing the satirical songs he set to folk tunes.

His songs were photographs of truth, and they voiced their opinions without fear of anyone. There was, it seems, a great landlord in Thirukkuvalai known as the Kuthagaikkara Iyer—the leaseholder Iyer. Everyone lived in fear and trembling before him. At that time a song arose as the voice of the poor. My father wrote it against that lord and sang it aloud, beginning with these lines:

If you inflict such cruelty, what are we poor to do?
We will bear it no longer—
we shall turn into spears, into lances!
The whole village, it seems, began singing it; and little by little the leaseholder's swagger subsided.

A woman from a prominent family had strayed from the accepted path. She had taken up with many lovers. Unable to bear the pain, her husband had entered a monastery and become a thambiran. The sexual adventures of this woman from a great household multiplied. Many of the village's important men were caught in her net.

My father felt that this had to be condemned, that it had to be opposed. Among those who deserved his condemnation were several of his own relatives. Those who had strayed from the path were attacked by the poet Muthuvel. Without concealing even an atom of the naked truth, he wrote a song to the tune called 'Elelo!' I wish to give only a few lines. The poem is written as though the woman herself were singing to her husband:

What if the neighbours see?
What if they say I have committed a sin?
What if the whole region comes to know?
What if honour and reputation are gone?
Listening to your mother's words, you tied the thali;
you befriended the goldsmith—and left me with him!
Thinking women themselves were goddesses, you were ruined;
you acquired habits and ways that were not fit for you—

The wife scolds her husband in this fashion. And then, to him, she describes the splendours of the sexual adventures she herself carried on with others. The husband has a good house and every comfort; yet she enters the temple with one of her illicit lovers. My father turns that episode into verse:

Though you had a whole village under lease,
though the burdens of your own household stood over your head,
though you had separate buildings and a pleasure-house of your own,
I went straight into Tyagesa's sacrificial hall;
there I saw the obscenity with my own eyes,
hastily gathering up the end of my sari, I stood;
I drank all the drink from the nectar-cup,
then hurriedly climbed the wall, leapt down and went away.
Was the game over with that?

From there I went into the room in the maiden-corner;
there I saw the handsome Velappa Sami.
I dallied and mingled with him and came away.
To whom shall I tell the strange sport that happened there?
Oh mother—you're the one who must listen!
The song goes on still further. It is very long. I do not now wish to quote all the lines in which the heroine is named and the qualities of the lovers who fell for her are painted in detail.

That is to say, I admit that I do not possess the courage my father possessed. Is it not astonishing that a man who had grown up an orphan, with little support from anyone, could many years ago stand alone in a small village and acquire the strength to condemn everyone who deserved it? And openly to ridicule those called the great men of the village—the heads of religious establishments and the retainers around them—was dangerous indeed. Yet he undertook it with courage.

For all this, my father was a thoroughgoing devotee of God! Whether dawn itself had broken or not, sacred ash would already have climbed onto his forehead. Many people also came to him believing him to be an accomplished manthirikar, a practitioner of mantras. For snakebite, scorpion sting and serious wounds, crowds would gather around Muthuvel the manthirikar.

He would chant a mantra, bind on medicine, and send them away. Whether the illness left because of the medicine or because of the mantra—even he did not know. He believed that doing the two together was what constituted the magic. He accepted no offering from anyone for it. If someone insisted on giving something, he would ask that bottles of toddy be placed as an offering in the name of a puja called 'placing milk for Idumban Sami.' This Idumban puja took place once every two months at the sacred tank opposite our house.

A manthirikar, a vidwan, a hardworking farmer and a man of learning—such was my father. He was married when he was still very young. A woman had waited, determined that it was he whom she wished to marry. The marriage took place as she desired. Within a few years of the marriage, my father lost his wife. Yes; we lost our elder mother.

My father lamented that Kunjammal, that lamp of the lineage, had been extinguished. Yet that lamp remained in his heart as an inextinguishable flame and became his family deity. In a beautiful little box he preserved the garland she had worn on their wedding day and made his first wife his own family deity. That box, with the flower garlands our father placed inside it, remains in our house even today.
He married a second time. He lost that wife too. Her name was Vedhammal. Third, Anjugam became his wife.

Our deity of love—the great woman who bore us and raised us—the gold who laboured like an ant and made something of us—our mother, whom we could call 'Amma!' with our whole mouths and find joy and comfort in that very call—our mother, precious as rare medicine, who gave us the inner richness and strength to build and guard a large household over which peace could dwell!

When she became his good companion in life, happiness sprouted once more in my father's heart. Along with the many difficulties he already bore came the heavy responsibility of tending the cultivation. Even though he was not in a position where he had to earn his living through hard labour, my father would take the plough and go to the fields. My mother too would join in the fieldwork to help him. Planting seedlings, weeding—she worked at these tasks alongside the other labourers.

Everything needed for the paddy field was kept in our house, not one thing missing, each item in proper order. From the stick used to drive the cattle to the plank used to strike a snake, everything was neatly maintained.

Fishing with a hook was one of my father's recreations. There were different hooks in the house for different fish: one for the varal, another for the kendai, and so on. In our coconut grove there was no need to hire a man to pluck coconuts. Our house had long hooked poles called thurattis, longer than the coconut trees themselves. Standing on the ground, Appa would use them to pluck the coconuts.
Once, while he was doing this, a great tender coconut dropped straight onto his head. Nothing happened to the coconut! And nothing happened to Appa's head either.
For many years Muthuvelar and Anjugam suffered from the sorrow of having no children. A Kural kept echoing in my father's heart:

Sweeter even than nectar is the gruel
in which one's children have dabbled
with their little hands.

However sorrowfully one may sit in the hall, looking at a pot of gruel and sighing, if at that moment a child playing on the veranda thrusts its tender little hand into the pot, does not that gruel become nectar? Appa and Amma were afflicted by the sorrow of having no little bud with the power to turn it into nectar.

Later they had two daughters, Periya Nayagam and Shanmugasundaram. Yet they were not satisfied. Deeply troubled that they had no male child, they visited sacred places. They bathed in holy waters. They undertook severe fasts.

Then came Salivahana Era 1846, Kali Era 5025, Kollam 1099—the corresponding Raktakshi year—the twenty-first day of the month of Vaikasi, a Tuesday; that is, the third of June 1924. On that auspicious day, under an auspicious conjunction, a child was born to Muthuvelar and Anjugathammal.
That child was I.
While I was still an infant, my mother lost her thali—the marriage pendant. My father had not died. Yet my mother lost her thali!

It was early one morning. I was asleep, still an infant. Father, mother and my sisters too were in deep sleep. Choosing precisely that moment, thieves entered the house. They swept away every vessel and possession in it, leaving nothing behind. They did not even spare the cloth of the cradle in which I lay. They must have been beggars even among thieves!

Poor fellows, they even cut away the golden thali glittering around the neck of my mother as she slept deeply. Until the day she died, my mother would tell me: 'It was fortunate that you did not cry when the thieves entered. If you had cried, they might have strangled you before leaving.'
Whenever Amma told me that, I used to think: 'Alas! Why didn't I cry then? If I had, I would not now have to suffer troubles coming at me from all four sides!'
The thieves went away after looting everything in the house except us. Only after they had gone, it seems, did our watchdog begin to bark!

My mother woke, found the thali missing from her neck, and rolled about weeping. At once my father comforted her: 'But I am still here! Why are you crying?' And he tied another thali around Amma's neck.
So our Appa tied four thalis for three wives!
'He even stole the thali!' Amma is said to have exclaimed in distress. Appa answered: 'Yes! If the thali had been made of brass, the thief might have thought,
and left it untouched. But the thali was made of gold, wasn't it? He must have decided that there is no sin in gold!'
That was how he offered a philosophy even for theft.
